identification.title: Hymn of Heaven
identification.notes: Written by Phil Wickham with Bill Johnson, Brian Johnson and Chris Davenport. Widely used since release and among the more doctrinally substantial songs in current rotation.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses over a repeated chorus with an outro. The verses move from the present longing, through the removal of sorrow, to the gathered worship of heaven; the chorus is the song sung there.

claims.claim: A day is coming when tears are wiped away and pain ceases.
claims.subject: The new creation

claims.claim: The one worshipped there is he who died and rose again.
claims.subject: The resurrection
claims.lyricExcerpt: He who died and rose again

claims.claim: Every knee will bow and every tongue confess him.
claims.subject: Universal acknowledgement

claims.claim: The singer will stand face to face with God among the saints and angels.
claims.subject: The vision of God

claims.claim: Christ's sacrifice is what makes forgiveness possible.
claims.subject: The atonement

strengths.title: Heaven described from Scripture rather than imagined
strengths.explanation: Tears wiped away, pain ended, every knee bowed: the song's picture of heaven comes from Revelation and Philippians rather than from speculation about what it might be like.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He will wipe away every tear; death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning or crying or pain.

strengths.title: The object of heaven's worship is the crucified and risen Christ
strengths.explanation: The chorus does not leave the one worshipped abstract. Naming him as the one who died and rose keeps the song's future anchored in a past event rather than in a hope about the future generally.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: He who died and rose again
strengths.scriptureRationale: Worthy are you, for you were slain and by your blood ransomed people for God.

strengths.title: Says why the singer may be there
strengths.explanation: The song grounds its hope in Christ's sacrifice rather than assuming the singer's place in heaven. That single move separates it from most songs about the life to come.
strengths.scriptureRationale: We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus.

strengths.title: The hope is a crowd, not a solitary arrival
strengths.explanation: Saints and angels are present, and the song is one the whole company sings. It resists the individualism that usually shapes songs about heaven.
strengths.scriptureRationale: A great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, standing before the throne.

concerns.title: All prayer characterised as crying out in pain
concerns.explanation: The second verse frames the present life's prayers as cries of despair. Much prayer is that; much is thanksgiving, confession and intercession. As a description of the singer's whole prayer life it is narrower than Scripture's.
concerns.scriptureRationale: In everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving — a wider range than lament alone.

doctrinesAffirmed: The death and resurrection of Christ
The atonement as the ground of access
The gathered worship of the redeemed
theological.assessment: One of the better songs about heaven in current use, largely because it declines to speculate. Its picture comes from Revelation and Philippians, the one worshipped there is named as the crucified and risen Christ, and it says why the singer may be present at all. The hope is corporate rather than solitary. One line narrows prayer to lament, which is a small imprecision in an otherwise careful song.

strengths.title: A song the whole company sings
strengths.explanation: Both the content and the grammar are corporate: the room joins a crowd already singing rather than describing a private experience.

strengths.title: For a grieving church
strengths.explanation: It gives a congregation that has buried someone a forward look grounded in a real event, without asking them to feel better than they do.

strengths.title: A chorus a room keeps
strengths.explanation: Short, repeated, and built on a phrase that is easy to hold. Congregations sing this one rather than watching it.

concerns.title: The outro sits high and sustains
concerns.explanation: The song's closing section is written for a lead voice and holds above where most rooms are comfortable. Congregations carry the verses and hand back the climax.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in A and B flat. The outro is the demanding part; pitch for that rather than for the opening verse.

range.key: Commonly published in A and B flat
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus and outro repeat substantially, and what repeats names the crucified and risen Christ. The repetition carries content rather than sustaining a mood.
communal.assessment: Well made for a congregation and corporate in both content and grammar. Its practical limit is the outro, which is written for a lead voice and sits above where most rooms will follow.

strengths.title: The one worshipped is named
strengths.explanation: By identifying him as the one who died and rose, the song rules out any vaguer reading of who is being sung to. That is not universal in songs about heaven.

strengths.title: Present and future kept distinct
strengths.explanation: The song is careful about what is now and what is then rather than blurring them into general hopefulness. A hearer follows the sequence easily.

concerns.title: A grammatical slip in the third verse
concerns.explanation: The line about standing face to face uses a subject pronoun where an object is required. It is a small thing, and it is the kind of thing a congregation sings hundreds of times.

clarity.assessment: Clear and well sequenced, with the object of worship named rather than implied. The only blemish is a grammatical slip in the third verse, which affects polish rather than meaning.

synthesis.summary: One of the better songs about heaven in current use, largely because it declines to speculate: its picture comes from Revelation and Philippians, the one worshipped is named as the crucified and risen Christ, and it says why the singer may be there at all. One line narrows prayer to lament, which is a small imprecision in an otherwise careful song.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Tears wiped away and pain ended — the picture the first verse takes directly.
The slain Lamb as the object of heaven's song, which the chorus names.
Confidence to enter by the blood of Jesus — the ground the song supplies.
Prayer as wider than lament, which the second verse narrows.
